full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This Rule at the instance of the petitioner Crescent Jute Mills Company Ltd. was issued calling upon the respondents Chairman, Labour Court, Khulna and the complainant Md. Abdul Hoque Khan to show cause as to why judgment and order dated 30-1-1988 passed by the Labour Court, in Misc. Case No. 19 of 1985 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 2. Mr. Khalilur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner after placing the impugned judgment and other materials on record submitted that respondent No. 2 filed Complaint Case No. 132 of 1983 under section 25(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 complaining against his dismissal from service and praying for re-instatement with back wages. The case was rejected by order dated 11-4-1984 as he failed to appear before the Labour Court not being a civil Court has no jurisdiction to set aside an order of dismissal for default under the provisions of Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, Labour Court acted illegally in passing the impugned judgment setting aside the order of dismissal and restoring the complaint case to its original file and number. In support of his contention learned Advocate relied on the decision in the case of Pubali Bank vs. Chairman, 1st. Labour Court, Dhaka and another reported in 44 DLR (AD) 40. 

 3. It appears from the materials on record that respondent No.2 filed the aforesaid complaint case alleging that he was implicated in a false criminal case and was discharged from that case and thereafter a departmental proceedings was started against him. In that departmental proceeding witnesses were not examined in his presence and he was not given chance to closse examine them in a malafide manner and his past service record was not also considered and as such order of dismissal was illegal. In that case on 11-4-1984 none of the parties appeared. So the Labour Court rejected the complainant's application. Thereafter he filed an application under Order 9, rule 4 read with section 151 of the Code of CiviI Procedure praying for restoration of the case by setting aside the order of rejection on the ground that he was ill and had to leave his Khalishpur residence and go to his village home and was under treatment for a long time and, as such, he could neither contact his Lawyer nor appear before the Court and after his recovery he came to Khulna and came to know about the order of rejection and then filed the case. That application was contested by the petitioner denying the material allegations and asserting that application was not maintainable under Order 9, Rule 4 or section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. After considering the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties Labour Court allowed the case holding that due to illness respondent No. 2 could not appear before the court and, as such, there was sufficient reason for his non-appearance and for ends of justice he should be given an opportunity to contest the case. 

 4. Labour Court is constituted under section 35 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 and procedures to be followed by the Labour Court have been mentioned in section 36 of the said Ordinance. Under the provision of section 2(K) of the Employment of Labour(Standing Orders) Act, 1965 for the purpose of deciding complaint cases under section 25 of that Act the Labour Court constituted under the said Ordinance is the Labour Court. 

 (d) In deciding the matter the court may pass such order including orders regarding cost, as it may deem, just and proper and it may, in appropriate case, require, by such order, the reinstatements of the complaint thereof and such order, shall be final. 

 5. From the above it appears that Labour Court while deciding a complaint case shall give notice and hearing to the parties and in deciding the complaint case Labour Court may pass any order as it deems just and proper including order regarding cost and reinstatement of the complainant. Except the above procedure no other procedure for deciding the complaint case has been provided in the said Act nor procedure provided under section 36 of the Ordinance has been adopted for the purpose of adjudicating complaint cases under section 25 of the Act. 

 6. Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act is a benificial legislation enacted for the purpose of protecting interests, of the workers in the Industrial and Commercial Establishments. Section 25 gives a worker right to seek remedy before the Labour Court against his dismissal, discharge, retrenchment, layoff or removal from service' in any other manner and also against his termination if it was due to his trade union activities or for recovery of his termination benefits. Clause (c) referred to herein before authorises the Labour Court to decide the complaint after giving notice and hearing to the parties. To give the decision Labour Court is required to go into the merit of the case by examining witnesses and documents. The question is whether Labour Court can dismiss a case for default for non-appearance of the complainant and thereafter vacate such order to decide the matter after hearing the parties. In the absence of any power under the provisions of Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that Labour Court constituted under section 35 of the IRO is not a civil Court and cannot exercise power under Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside an order of dismissal for default of a complaint case. Question before the Appellant Division in the aforesaid case reported in 44 DLR was that whether the Labour Court could pass an order of stay of transfer order till disposal of the IRO case. In deciding that case it was held that Labour Court in adjudicating and determining an industrial dispute acts as a civil Court for a limited purpose and it will not exercise power like those given under Order 9 or Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure which the civil Court may exercise in a suit but are in no sense necessary for deciding an industrial dispute. In view of the aforesaid decision Labour Court adjudicating an industrial dispute cannot exercise powers given under the Provisions of Order 9 of the Code of Civil procedure to set aside order of dismissal for default or allowing the case ex-parte. 

 7. Under the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 36 of IRO Labour Court shall follows as nearly as possible summary Procedure. Section 262 of the Code of Criminal procedure provides that procedure prescribed in Chapter XX shall be followed in summary trials, sections 241 to 250 of the said Code fall under Chapter XX. Section 247 under Chapter XX provides that if the complainant fails to appear on the date of hearing the Magistrate shall acquit the accused unless for some reasons he thinks proper to adjourn the hearing of the case to some other day. According to the learned Advocate for the petitioner in exercise of this power Labour Court is competent to pass an order for dismissal for default or rejection of a complaint petition for non-appearance of the complainant On the other hand, Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate appearing as Amicus Curiae submitted that since the provisions of section 36 of the IRO have not been adopted in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act either expressly or by necessary implication these provisions will not apply in respect of the complaint case. But he concedes that if a party does not appear before the Labour Court in spite of notice Labour Court cannot wait indefinitely for his appearance and would be justified in passing an order of dismissal for default or rejection of the complaint if the complainant failed to appear though Labour Court deciding a complaint case has no such power under Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But he further contends that if the defaulting party can satisfy the Labour Court as to the cause of his non-appearance then Labour Court is competent to pass an order to restore the case after setting aside the order of dismissal for default or rejection of the complaint petition to give a hearing to that party for deciding the case on merit and such power is ancillary or incidental to the power of the Labour Court to decide the complaint case. 

 8. After hearing the learned Advocates we find that the petitioner did not file any written statement before the Labour Court in complaint case No. 132 of 1983 and on 11-4-1984 petitioner also did not appear before the Labour Court. But the Labour Court rejected the complaint case as the complainant -respondent No.2 failed to take steps in spite of several notices. 

 9. From the impugned judgment it appears that respondent No.2 could not appear before the Labour Court due to his illness which was supported by medical evidence. So the Labour Court set aside the aforesaid order of rejection and restored the complaint case to give a chance to him to contest the complaint case. In our view the case was restored to give a chance to the respondent No.2 to substantiate his case so that Labour Court could give decision in the case on merit after hearing the parties. Without setting aside or vacting the said order of rejection Labour Court could not decide the complaint case on merit. Since under section 25(c) Labour Court has been empowered to decide the complaint case giving the parties notice and hearing and under section 25(d) is empowered to pass any order deemed just and proper Labour Court has jurisdiction to set aside or vacate the order of dismissal for default or rejection of the complaint. Since the petitioner neither filed written statement nor appeared before the Labour Court on the date the complaint petition was rejected we are of the view that petitioner cannot be said to have suffered any loss by the order of restoration and, as such, cannot be aggrieved by the them. Since the overriding responsibility of the Labour Court is to decide the complaint case after giving notice and hearing to the parties it had no option but to set aside the order of rejection for non-appearance of the complainant who was able to satisfy the Labour Court as to the cause of his non-appearance. Deciding a case means deciding it on merit and not by passing a default order. 

 10. In a different context a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Chand Miah Talukdar vs. Chairman, Court of Settlement and another reported in 45 DLR 304 held that Court of settlement is required to decide the case on merit and was not authorised to dismiss the case for default in the absence of such power and hence remanded the case to the Court of Settlement for deciding the same on merit. We agree with the ratio ratiodecidendi of that case and find support to our above view in that decision. 

 11. It is true that Labour Court while deciding a complaint case is not a Civil Court and cannot exercise power under Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Still it has ancillary and indidental power to pass appropriate order required in the facts and circumstances of the case under section 25 of the said Act and, as such, impugned order cannot be said to be without jurisdiction. Since provisions of section 36 of the IRO has not been adopted in the said Act in deciding a complaint case Labour Court is to follow the procedure mentioned in section 25 of the Act and not summary procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure. It appears Labour Court wrongly exercised the power under Order 9 rule 4 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But such wrong exercise of power under a provision of law not lying with the Labour Court cannot affect its jurisdiction under the provisions of section 25 of the Act as found above.
